column4: The disciples want the table so that “our hearts may be reassured” and so they may know that Jesus has spoken truth; trusted speech and a settled heart meet explicitly.
Faith is denied until the hearers accept the Prophet as judge, find no inward unease at his decision, and submit fully; belief, accepted judgment, and inward rest are one sequence.
God makes those who believe firm through “the firm word” (ٱلْقَوْلِ ٱلثَّابِتِ), directly joining accepted speech to settledness.
Those given knowledge recognize revelation as truth, believe it, and let their hearts yield to it; this is the heart’s response to God making His signs firm in 22:52.
Joseph’s brothers concede, “you will not believe us, even if we are truthful,” making belief precisely the acceptance of a speaker’s truthfulness.
The brothers bring Joseph’s shirt with “false blood” (بِدَمٍ كَذِبٍ); a fabric’s visible state participates in a lie, closely enacting the section’s deceptive-cloth sense.
God distinguishes calling the Prophet a liar from rejecting God’s signs: “they do not call you false” (لَا يُكَذِّبُونَكَ), directly illuminating the alternate personal object in 95:7.
One person invents a lie against God and also denies the truth when it arrives, bringing fabrication and rejection into the same act.
The one who brings truth and the one who confirms it (وَصَدَّقَ بِهِ) form the positive pair of trustworthy word and believing reception.
When the believers see the confederates, the feared event verifies God’s and the Messenger’s promise; they answer “God and His Messenger spoke true,” and their faith increases.
At resurrection the sleepers recognize, “This is what the Merciful promised, and the messengers spoke truth,” so the once-contested promise publicly vindicates its speakers.
“Rather, you deny the Judgment” (تُكَذِّبُونَ بِٱلدِّينِ) is the closest independent formulation of the denial named in 95:7.
The Prophet is asked to look at the person who “denies the Judgment,” restaging 95:7 as an observable human type.
The transgressors are identified as those who deny the Day of Judgment, giving the object of the denial its eschatological setting.
On the Day itself they are told, “This is what you used to deny”; the cited ayah supplies the encounter with what 83:11 says they rejected.
The people of the Fire confess that they used to deny the Day of Judgment, turning present denial into retrospective self-testimony.
The question “What if he denies and turns away?” immediately after surah 95 pairs false judgment of the message with conduct that enacts the rejection.
When one person trusts another, the entrusted person must discharge the trust (أَمَٰنَتَهُ); the ayah states interpersonal confidence and its opposite, betrayal, in the section’s own root.
Believers are forbidden to betray God, the Messenger, or their trusts, exactly realizing the dictionary opposition between amānah and treachery.
God commands trusts to be returned to their owners and judgments to be made justly, joining amānah to the judging function of 95:8.
Al-Muʾmin (ٱلْمُؤْمِنُ) appears as a divine name, directly supplying the section’s named sense of God as guarantor of His word.
Believing hearts find reassurance in God’s remembrance, explicitly stating the section’s definition of security as inward settledness.
Abraham already believes, yet asks to see resurrection “so that my heart may be reassured”; faith and the heart’s further settling are distinguished without being opposed.
A person coerced into an outward word of unbelief remains excepted when the heart is “secure in faith” (مُطْمَئِنٌّۢ بِٱلْإِيمَٰنِ), separating verbal appearance from inward truth.
God sends tranquility into believers’ hearts so that they increase in faith, directly joining sakīnah, heart, and īmān.
God makes the House a place repeatedly returned to and a security (أَمْنًا), combining dependable return, staying, and sanctuary around the place sworn by in 95:3.
Abraham asks God to make “this a secure city” (بَلَدًا ءَامِنًا), the closest syntactic and spatial counterpart to “this secure city” in 95:3.
Abraham again asks, “make this city secure,” tying the demonstrative city to security and protection from false worship.
God “made them safe from fear” (ءَامَنَهُم مِّنْ خَوْفٍ), almost glossing the section’s definition of security as fear’s removal.
God promises believers that He will replace their fear with security; the divine promise itself bears the meaning attributed to al-Muʾmin.
Those who believe without clothing their faith in wrongdoing are the ones to whom security belongs, placing the two branches of ء م ن in one sentence.
God verifies His Messenger’s true vision by promising entry into the Sacred Mosque “secure” and without fear, joining a fulfilled divine word to safety.
The objection that following guidance would cause abduction is answered by God’s establishment of a secure sanctuary, exposing fear as resistance to a trustworthy word.
Whoever enters the House is safe, giving the secure-place image of 95:3 a concrete sanctuary rule.
Noah introduces himself to his deniers as “a trustworthy messenger,” the exact messenger formula developed by the section.
Noah’s people deny the messengers; this row supplies the rejecting response to the trustworthy self-identification in 26:107.
Hud repeats “I am to you a trustworthy messenger,” showing that trustworthiness belongs to the recurring office, not merely one personality.
ʿĀd deny the messengers, providing the rejection to which Hud’s claim of trustworthiness in 26:125 answers.
Ṣāliḥ gives the same “trustworthy messenger” self-description before delivering his demand for obedience.
Thamud deny the messengers, forming the denial half of the trust-and-rejection scene completed in 26:143.
Lot identifies himself as a trustworthy messenger, again locating amānah in the bearer of the divine word.
Lot’s people deny the messengers; 26:162 separately answers that denial with the messenger’s trustworthy status.
Shuʿayb repeats the trustworthy-messenger formula, here before a people whose practice also falsifies measure.
The people of the thicket deny the messengers, supplying the response against which 26:178 asserts trustworthiness.
The trustworthy Spirit brings the revelation down, extending reliability from the human messenger to the message’s heavenly carrier.
The revelatory messenger is obeyed and trustworthy, confirming the reliability of the transmission before human acceptance or denial.
Moses addresses Pharaoh’s people as “a trustworthy messenger,” making his demand rest explicitly on the speaker’s reliability.
Hud calls himself “a trustworthy adviser,” showing amīn as the quality that warrants accepting admonitory speech.
After Joseph’s truthfulness has been disclosed, the king declares him established and trustworthy, making tested speech the ground of entrusted office.
The woman recommends Moses as strong and trustworthy after observing his conduct, so the character judgment rests on deed rather than self-display.
The jinn offers to bring the throne and says he is strong and trustworthy for the task, making amānah reliability in carrying out a promised act.
Abraham tells his people that they “create a falsehood” (تَخْلُقُونَ إِفْكًا), the exact named sense in which creating becomes fabricating.
The chiefs dismiss the proclamation of one God as nothing but fabrication (ٱخْتِلَٰقٌ), falsely assigning inventedness to revelation.
Inventing a lie against God and denying His signs are paired as the two gravest wrongs, joining fabricated speech to rejection of true speech.
The Book’s signs are “made firm” (أُحْكِمَتْ) and then detailed by the Wise, directly applying the firmness sense of حكم to trustworthy revelation.
God removes what Satan casts into prophetic recitation and then makes His signs firm; 22:54 shows knowledge, faith, and humbled hearts as the result.
Firm verses are the Book’s foundation, while deviant hearts chase ambiguity; those rooted in knowledge answer “We believe in it,” joining firm word and stable reception.
Noah invokes God as “the wisest of judges” while appealing to a promise; God’s ruling in the next ayah clarifies rather than breaks the promise.
Joseph’s eldest brother vows not to leave the land until his father permits him or God judges; remaining in place and waiting for divine حكم unite the section’s two final dictionary images.
“Is God not sufficient for His servant?” demands a settled yes while others try to frighten the Prophet, matching the secure answer sought by 95:8.
“What has deceived you concerning your generous Lord?” opens a sequence that recalls creation in 82:7 and identifies denial of judgment in 82:9.
God created, proportioned, and balanced the human being; this creation is the evidence immediately preceding 82:9’s denial of Judgment, closely paralleling 95:4–7.
The human created from a drop becomes an open adversary, staging true creation as the basis that should have prevented argumentative denial.
The objector forgets his own creation and produces a challenge about reviving bones, turning createdness into a fabricated argument against return.
The answer appeals to the One who created the bones the first time, identifying the real Maker against the human’s denying speech in 36:78.
“Is not” the Creator of the heavens and earth able to recreate them? “Yes” makes the stable response explicit and names Him the all-knowing Creator.
After rehearsing the human’s creation, “Is He not able to revive the dead?” uses the same fixed-answer form as 95:8 to answer denial of return.
“Were they created from nothing, or are they the creators?” forces denial back onto the question of which making is real.
“This is God’s creation; show Me what those besides Him created” sets actual making against unsupported claims for rivals.
The hypocrites utter a proposition that is factually true, yet God witnesses that they are liars; their stance makes their speech false despite its surface.
Their bodies impress and their speech attracts hearing, yet they are likened to propped timber; outward pattern and inward reality diverge like the section’s deceptive fabric.
A person’s speech about worldly life impresses and he calls God to witness his heart, while he is actually the fiercest opponent; 2:205 exposes the deed behind the display.
Once the impressive speaker turns away, he destroys crops and offspring; this ayah supplies the action that falsifies the words described in 2:204.
Believers are asked why they say what they do not do, making the truth-value of speech answerable to action.
God greatly hates saying what one does not do; this gives the moral verdict on the word-and-deed fracture named in 61:2.
The Bedouins’ verbal “we believe” is corrected because faith has not entered their hearts, directly separating a claim of belief from inward assent.
Those who stayed behind “say with their tongues what is not in their hearts,” a precise instance of the section’s lie in both utterance and act.
The hypocrites say with their mouths what is absent from their hearts, locating the instability of speech in a divided interior.
Some say “we believe” with their mouths while their hearts do not believe, and they distort words, combining false profession with corrupted transmission.
People say they believe in God and the Last Day although they are not believers, exposing a profession whose state contradicts its wording.
Disease in their hearts grows and punishment follows because they lie; this supplies the inward condition behind the false profession of 2:8.
People say “we believe and obey,” then a group turns away, so conduct refuses the word their mouths accepted.
When called to God and the Messenger for judgment, a group turns away; the ayah makes rejection of the judge the action behind 24:47’s false profession.
The refusers are asked whether their hearts are diseased, they doubt, or they fear injustice from God and His Messenger; unstable heart and distrust of judgment coincide.
The believers’ stable response when called for judgment is simply “we hear and we obey,” the accepting counterpart to 24:47–50.
People claim belief in revelation while seeking judgment from false authority, making their chosen judge contradict their spoken īmān.
When told to come to God’s revelation and the Messenger, the hypocrites turn away; their act verifies the false claim exposed in 4:60.
Believers who dispute are commanded to refer the matter back (فَرُدُّوهُ) to God and the Messenger, turning “return” into trust in the authoritative word.
“The heart did not lie about what it saw” (مَا كَذَبَ ٱلْفُؤَادُ), bringing the lying root directly into a claim about the heart’s faithful witness.
True believers are those who believe and then do not doubt, defining faith by the absence of the oscillation displayed in 9:45.
Moses’ mother nearly discloses him, but God binds her heart so that she may remain among the believers; firmness preserves faith under fear.
God strengthens the youths’ hearts when they stand and declare their Lord, joining an anchored heart to courageous truthful speech.
Messenger-stories are related to make the Prophet’s heart firm, and in them truth, admonition, and reminder arrive together.
The Qur’an is revealed gradually to strengthen the Prophet’s heart, so the trustworthy word itself produces inward steadiness.
Those who say “Our Lord is God” and then remain upright are told not to fear and are given the promised Garden; stable word and removed fear coincide.
Those who say “Our Lord is God” and remain upright have no fear or grief, closely joining settled commitment to the root meaning of security.
For the believing friends of God, His words cannot be changed; this grounds the good news and freedom from fear stated in 10:62–63.
“God’s promise is true” is followed by warnings against being deceived by worldly life or the deceiver, setting reliable promise against misleading appearance.
After promising believers lasting gardens, the ayah asks, “Who is truer than God in speech?” directly grounds faith in the reliability of His promise.
The certain gathering for Resurrection is sealed by “Who is truer than God in statement?”, joining Judgment to the Speaker’s unsurpassable truthfulness.
The people of Paradise praise God for making His promise true, presenting fulfillment as the public verification of the trusted divine word.
The people of Paradise and Fire each confirm that they found their Lord’s promise true, and a caller judges the wrongdoers.
Asked whether the promised punishment is really true, the Prophet answers by his Lord that it is certainly true and inescapable.
The Lord’s word is completed in truth and justice and none can alter His words, combining reliable speech with settled finality.
Divine help is made good news so believers’ hearts may be reassured by it; the promised sign serves inward rest.
The angelic aid is only good news “so that your hearts may be reassured,” repeating the same promise-to-settled-heart relation in battle.
In the cave the Prophet says “Do not grieve; God is with us,” and God sends down tranquility, so a trusted reassurance becomes experienced calm.
God knows what is in the pledgers’ hearts and sends tranquility upon them, joining tested loyalty, inward knowledge, and settledness.
Against pagan zeal, God sends tranquility upon His Messenger and believers and binds them to the word of piety; calm and a binding word answer agitation.
God sends drowsiness as security from Him, cleanses the believers, binds their hearts, and makes their feet firm; inward and outward steadiness are one gift.
Joseph’s brothers ask their father why he does not trust them with Joseph; their later false report in 12:17–18 exposes the requested trust as betrayed.
Jacob asks whether he should entrust Benjamin to the brothers as he entrusted Joseph before, making remembered betrayal govern renewed confidence.
The believers guard their trusts and covenants, giving action as the proof of the reliability named by amānah.
Guarding trusts and covenants recurs among the qualities of those stable in prayer, again making trustworthiness a practiced state.
The Trust is offered to creation and borne by the human being, enlarging amānah from an interpersonal deposit into a weighty moral charge.
People are not left merely to say “we believe” without trial; the spoken profession must be tested.
Trial makes manifest those who are truthful and those who lie, supplying the verdict on the profession stated in 29:2.
Rejecting false authority and believing in God is grasping a firm handhold that never breaks, rendering stable faith as physical attachment.
One who submits to God while doing good has grasped the firmest handhold; trust becomes settled reliance with enacted goodness.
In the crisis hypocrites and diseased hearts say God and His Messenger promised only delusion; 33:22 answers with the believers’ declaration that both spoke true.
Those who affirm the Day of Judgment (يُصَدِّقُونَ بِيَوْمِ ٱلدِّينِ) are the direct positive reversal of those who deny it.
Those seeking exemption have doubting hearts and “waver in their doubt,” the explicit opposite of the settled heart implied by security and faith.
The edge-worshipper is reassured by benefit but turns completely when tested, portraying a conditional calm that never becomes rooted faith.
Being turned back after guidance is pictured as a bewildered person wandering while companions call him to guidance, directly enacting the section’s lost, back-and-forth sense of ردد.
The hypocrites are “wavering between” two sides and belong fully to neither, a nonlexical portrait of the unsettled heart.
Moses flees without looking back, unlike the source-section animal that stops to look behind; he is then called forward and told not to fear because he is safe.
At the staff’s movement Moses turns fleeing and does not look back, and God answers the flight with “Do not fear,” repeating the boundary between panic and divine security.
A town once secure and inwardly at ease rejects God’s favors, so God clothes it in hunger and fear; security, denial, garment, and fear reverse within one image.
A messenger from the secure town’s own people comes, but they call him a liar; punishment then seizes them, explaining the reversal narrated in 16:112.
People see God make a secure sanctuary amid surrounding abduction, yet believe in falsehood and reject His favor; received safety does not settle their assent.
“Is one who creates like one who does not create?” draws the exact boundary between real making and objects falsely treated as makers.
The denier “neither confirmed nor prayed”; this negative prepares 75:32’s positive act of denial and contrasts with faith as tasdīq.
“He denied and turned away” makes rejection both a judgment about truth and an enacted withdrawal.
Confirming “the best” is the accepting response that leads toward ease, providing the positive side of the trust/denial divide.
Denying “the best” reverses 92:6 and leads toward hardship, so acceptance and rejection disclose their practical directions.
Breaking what they promised God and continuing to lie produces hypocrisy in their hearts, reversing the divine attribute of making a promise true.
Obedience and proper speech are demanded, but when the matter is resolved, truthfulness to God would be better; the testing act exposes the earlier words.
The hypocrites admit that they tempted themselves, waited, doubted, and were deceived by wishes until God’s command came, tracing an unsettled heart into fatal false confidence.
Those who do not expect the meeting with God become content and reassured by the nearer life; it is genuine settledness fixed on the wrong object.
Thamud are asked whether they expect to be left secure amid their gardens; their felt safety stands opposite their denial of the trustworthy messenger in 26:141–143.
The one cast into Fire is set against the one who arrives secure on Resurrection Day, making final judgment the boundary between apparent impunity and real safety.
Soon after Abraham names fabricated falsehood in 29:17, this ayah asks whether people see how God originates creation, locally setting actual creation against invention.
The command to travel and observe how creation began extends 29:19’s answer to the fabricated objects and stories rejected in 29:17.
Deniers dismiss the warning as “nothing but khuluq of the former peoples”; the disputed sense of خُلُق/خَلْق matters because inherited pattern is used to neutralize a true warning.
Shuʿayb asks God to judge truthfully between believers and deniers and calls Him the best of judges, placing divine حكم between accepted and rejected messenger-speech.
The Prophet is told to follow revelation and wait patiently until God judges, with God named the best of judges; trustworthy reception culminates in His decision.
The Prophet says judgment belongs only to God and that He relates the truth, joining true declaration to the decisive Judge.
When the judgment favors them, the same refusers come obediently; this selective acceptance exposes the instability diagnosed in 24:50.
Once God and His Messenger decide a matter, a believer has no residual choice, giving the settled form of accepting authoritative judgment.
After the rooted believers’ confession in 3:7, they ask God not to let their hearts deviate after guidance, naming stability as a continuing gift.
The Ark is given as a sign of kingship and contains tranquility from the Lord; an entrusted sign makes reassurance tangible.
The “reassured soul” is called to return to its Lord pleased and pleasing, showing settledness at the point when the divine promise is fulfilled.
After the believers’ confidence in their numbers fails them and they turn back, God sends tranquility upon the Messenger and believers; divine calm arrests retreat.
God’s allies have no fear or grief; 10:63 identifies them as believers, and 10:64 grounds their security in God’s unchangeable word.
The secure people of 10:62 are specifically those who believed and were mindful, while 10:64 supplies the reliable promise behind their state.
Some People of the Book wish to turn believers back into unbelief after faith; ردد becomes reversal from accepted truth to rejected truth.
Obeying a faction of the People of the Book would turn believers back to unbelief, warning that the wrong trusted speakers can reverse assent.
Obeying unbelievers would turn the believers back on their heels, turning trust in hostile counsel into loss.
The people described disbelieve after belief despite testifying that the Messenger is true, making rejected testimony a reversal of prior assent.
When a decisive surah (سُورَةٌ مُّحْكَمَةٌ) names fighting, diseased hearts look with deathly fear; a firm word reveals an unsteady interior.
What Satan casts becomes a trial for diseased and hardened hearts; this row supplies the unstable recipients contrasted with the knowing, believing hearts of 22:54.
God opens the breast of the one guided to submission and makes the breast of the misled constricted; this concretizes the source section’s “broad breast” sense of balda.
A breast opened to submission and illuminated by the Lord is contrasted with hardened hearts, developing the section’s broad-chest image into receptive faith.
Moses asks, “expand for me my breast,” so that he can deliver his difficult speech; an opened chest supports a trustworthy messenger’s utterance.
The Prophet is reminded that God expanded his breast, a bodily image of the inward capaciousness named under the root of balad.
The calf-worshippers say they will not cease clinging to it until Moses returns; steadfast nondeparture is attached to a false object, reversing the section’s desired fixed answer.
Moses says he will not cease until reaching the meeting of the two seas; persistence and water give a concrete parallel to the source dictionary’s animals that do not leave the pool.
The debt ayah regulates writing and witness so a disputed obligation can be trusted; this legal setting concretely approaches the section’s dictionary sense of crediting a person in adjudication.
Joseph’s plan proceeds under “the king’s law” (دِينِ ٱلْمَلِكِ), showing dīn in a judicial order rather than only the eschatological object denied in 95:7.
Reports of security or fear should be referred back to the Messenger and competent authorities, linking reliable news, proper return, and the two states defining amn.
The mindful are placed in a secure station, carrying the “remaining in a trusted place” side of the image into the final abode.
The people of the Garden are told to enter in peace and security, making removed fear a final settled condition.
Joseph tells his family to enter Egypt secure, closing a story driven by betrayed trust with safe reunion under his verified word.
The Prophet “believes in God and believes the believers,” using the same root first for faith and then for crediting people’s word; this directly exposes the section’s two linked senses.

Pharaoh’s believing kinsman weighs Moses’ claim: if Moses lies, the lie returns upon him, but if he is truthful, some promised consequence will strike; trusting a messenger is framed as a testable judgment.
A witness makes the direction of the tear in Joseph’s shirt adjudicate whether the woman is truthful and Joseph a liar; the cloth itself becomes evidence about speech.
The shirt torn from behind proves that the woman lied and Joseph told the truth, reversing the deceptive shirt of 12:18 into fabric that discloses reality.
Before the Fire the deniers say that, if returned, they would no longer deny the signs and would become believers; the row contributes their professed change of trust.
God says that if they were returned they would return to what was forbidden and that they are liars, joining both kinds of “return” to the exposure of a false promise in 6:27.
Abraham asks which of the two parties has the stronger right to security, after contrasting his lack of fear with his people’s fear; 6:82 gives the verdict for uncorrupted faith.
After naming himself a trustworthy messenger in 44:18, Moses says, “If you do not believe me, then leave me alone”; the cited ayah makes personal trust in the messenger the contested response.
Hud’s people say they think he is among the liars; his claim to be a trustworthy adviser in 7:68 directly answers this accusation.
Moses is restored to his mother so that her eye may be comforted, she may cease grieving, and she may know God’s promise is true; it completes the heart-strengthening act of 28:10.
The Holy Spirit brings the Qur’an down in truth to make those who believe firm, joining a reliable carrier, a true word, faith, and settledness in one ayah.
The accusation that the Prophet fabricated a lie is answered by God’s effacing falsehood and confirming truth with His words; fabricated and established speech are expressly separated.
The charge that the Prophet composed the revelation is answered, “Rather, they do not believe,” making alleged fabrication a form of refused faith.
Those alleging invented speech are challenged to produce a discourse like it “if they are truthful”; this ayah tests the speakers of the charge made in 52:33.
The possibility that the Messenger might fabricate sayings in God’s name is raised only to declare the consequence that would follow, sharply guarding the trustworthiness of transmitted revelation.
Inventing a lie against God includes falsely claiming revelation or claiming the ability to reveal like God; the death scene then exposes the pretended speaker.
People are forbidden to let their tongues falsely label things lawful or unlawful and thereby fabricate a lie against God; speech itself manufactures the false religious claim.
The builders of the harmful mosque swear that they intended only good, but God witnesses that they are liars; a pious-looking deed and its verbal defense are jointly false.
The hypocrites use their oaths as a shield and obstruct God’s way; this ayah supplies the action performed by the false testimony exposed in 63:1.
The slanderers’ failure to produce four witnesses means that before God they are the liars, showing a false report judged by an evidentiary standard.
A person says “we believe” but reverses under human persecution; the closing question asks whether God is not best aware of what hearts contain.
The judgment of ignorance is set against the question, “Who is better than God in judgment for people who are certain?”, a close counterpart to 95:8’s final appeal.
The Prophet asks whether he should seek a judge other than God when God has sent the Book fully explained; divine judgment and trusted revelation validate one another.
God judges with truth, whereas the beings invoked besides Him cannot judge anything; real judgment is distinguished from an empty attribution.
Earlier messengers endured being denied until God’s help came, and none can change God’s words; rejection by hearers cannot falsify the promise.
The Prophet must recite what is revealed because none can alter God’s words, presenting the divine utterance as fixed and dependable.
At judgment God states that the word is not changed in His presence and that He does not wrong servants; finality of speech and justice coincide.
The prayer affirms that God will gather humanity for an undoubted Day because God does not fail the appointment, directly linking Judgment to a reliable promise.
After God’s covenantal promise to believers, the ayah asks who is more faithful to a covenant than God, closely matching the named divine sense of al-Muʾmin.
God’s true promise of universal return is grounded in His originating and repeating creation so that He may judge and reward justly.
The ayah declares that God’s promise is true even though most people do not know, setting objective reliability against unsettled human recognition.
The Prophet must not think God will fail His promise to His messengers; divine vindication is guaranteed despite present denial.
Discovery of the sleepers is arranged so people may know that God’s promise is true and the Hour admits no doubt; an observed sign settles contested speech.
The unseen Gardens promised by the Merciful are assured because His promise is bound to arrive.
God promises to repeat creation as He began it and says the promise is binding upon Him and will be done, uniting true making with fulfilled speech.
“God’s promise—God does not fail His promise” states in repeated form the reliability attributed to the divine name al-Muʾmin.
God’s promise is true, while worldly life and the deceiver can delude; dependable word is set against misleading appearance and speech.
The promised lofty chambers are guaranteed with the statement that God does not fail the appointed promise.
The Prophet is told to be patient because God’s promise is true, so steadiness rests upon confidence in the divine word.
Whether the Prophet sees part of the threatened outcome or dies first, what God promises the deniers will come, making fulfillment independent of the hearer’s timetable.
The promised Day rends the sky, and God’s promise is described as accomplished; the judgment denied now becomes a completed event.
Those in doubt about the revealed word are challenged to produce a comparable surah and call their witnesses if they are truthful, turning suspicion into a public truth test.
Exclusive claims to Paradise are met with “Bring your proof, if you are truthful,” requiring a claimed religious word to bear evidence.
A frightening human report increases the believers’ faith, and they answer that God is sufficient and the best trustee; trusted reliance settles rather than amplifies the threat.
Believers are called to let their hearts become humble to God’s remembrance and the revealed truth, making the true word’s inward effect the issue.
Whoever believes in God has the heart guided by Him, directly joining īmān to the heart’s right placement under affliction.
When the listeners hear revelation, they recognize its truth and openly affirm belief, showing trustworthy speech arriving at sincere assent.
After recalling creation of the heavens and earth, the ayah asks whether God is not able to revive the dead and supplies “Yes” as the fixed response.
The question asks whether any alleged partner originates creation and repeats it; God alone does so, and the hearers are asked how they are turned away.
The human is commanded to consider from what he was created, beginning an evidentiary sequence that concludes with God’s power to return him in 86:8.
After naming the human’s created origin, the passage states that God is able to return him, making first creation evidence for the contested return.
Those who disbelieve claim they will not be raised; the Prophet must answer “Yes, by my Lord,” followed by certain informing and recompense.
Those who disbelieve say the Hour will not come; the Prophet answers “Yes, by my Lord,” grounding the fixed response in God’s knowledge.
People believe, disbelieve, believe again, and then deepen in disbelief; the repeated reversals enact an unrooted heart’s movement between assent and denial.
True believers’ hearts tremble when God is mentioned, yet recited signs increase their faith and reliance; bodily awe marks a boundary rather than the wavering doubt opposed by the section.
The best discourse first makes skins shiver, then skins and hearts soften to God’s remembrance; agitation resolves into receptive rest rather than indecision.
God tells the Prophet that divine strengthening kept him from inclining toward the pressure of opponents, marking firmness as protection against even a slight turn.
One who brings a good deed is safe from the terror of the Judgment Day, placing true security on the far side of accountable action.
Hud denies being foolish and identifies himself as a messenger from the Lord; this clears the false personal charge in 7:66 before 7:68 asserts his trustworthiness.
Immediately after Noah calls himself trustworthy, he commands his people to be mindful of God and obey him; the ayah states the response that amānah warrants.
Hud’s trustworthy-messenger declaration is followed by the repeated demand for obedience, making confidence in the bearer practical.
Ṣāliḥ follows his claim of trustworthiness with a command to heed and obey, distinguishing accepted messenger-speech from his people’s denial.
Lot’s declaration of amānah leads directly to the command to obey, giving the trusted word its demanded reception.
Shuʿayb’s trustworthy status likewise grounds the call to obey, completing the final repetition of the scene.
The claim that the Prophet fabricated the Qur’an is met by a challenge to produce ten comparable surahs and enlist any available helpers.
Those who say the Qur’an was fabricated are challenged to produce one comparable surah and call witnesses if truthful.
The accusation “he fabricated it” is rejected with the statement that it is truth from the Lord, sent to warn a previously unwarned people.
When opponents say the revelation was fabricated, the Prophet is told to acknowledge that fabrication would leave him helpless before God; God knows their hostile discourse.
The unbelievers call the Qur’an a lie invented with others’ help; the ayah itself judges that accusation an unjust falsehood.
At death the wrongdoer asks to be returned, supplying the requested reversal whose asserted purpose appears in 23:100.
The plea to return and act righteously is refused as “only a word he says,” exposing a late promise whose speech cannot establish trust.
At the final gathering the record is set down, prophets and witnesses are brought, and judgment is made in truth, publicly resolving contested testimony.
One who guides to truth is contrasted with one unable to find the way without guidance, and the hearers are challenged over how they judge.
Believers who support God’s cause are promised divine support and firmly planted feet, rendering faithful commitment as stability in action.
God tells the angels that He is with them and commands them to make the believers firm, presenting divine presence as the answer to battlefield fear.
Moses and Aaron are told not to fear because God is with them, hearing and seeing; the trusted divine assurance answers their apprehension before speaking to Pharaoh.
